title: Reason Through SAT Survey Questions
description: Evaluate survey samples, limit conclusions to the correct population, and interpret margin of error as a plausible range.

blocks.html:
Four decisions solve survey questions

SAT survey questions rarely require complicated calculations. They ask whether a sample is trustworthy, how far its results can be generalized, and what uncertainty remains.

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  1. identify the target population and sample,
  2. separate well-designed random samples from biased samples,
  3. choose a conclusion with the correct scope and certainty, and
  4. turn a margin of error into a plausible range.

Start with the selection method

A principal wants to estimate what all students at a high school think about a later start time.

Imagine four possible plans: ask students entering the library, post an optional poll on social media, randomly select students from the complete enrollment list, or ask only the student council.

Before learning the formal terms, decide which plan gives every kind of student the best chance to be represented.

content.prompt: Which plan is best designed to estimate the opinion of all students at the school?
choices: Ask the first 100 students who enter the library.
Post an optional poll on the school's social media account.
Randomly select students from the complete school enrollment list.
Ask every member of the student council.
content.hint: Look for a method that starts with the entire group of students and does not depend on volunteering or visiting one location.
content.explanation: Correct. A random selection from the complete enrollment list gives students across the school a chance to be included and avoids relying on one convenient or self-selected group.

blocks.html:
Name the group and the part you observe

  • The target population is the entire group the survey is trying to describe.
  • The sample is the smaller group that is actually selected and surveyed.
  • A sample statistic is a measured result from that sample, such as the percent who chose yes.
  • The corresponding population value is the unknown true percent for the whole target population.

Key idea: The sample result is known for the respondents. Using it to describe the population requires inference and uncertainty.

content.prompt: A random sample of 250 students is surveyed, and 64% of that sample supports a new schedule. Which statement is known from the survey data?
choices: Exactly 64% of the sampled students support the schedule.
Exactly 64% of every student at the school supports the schedule.
Every group of 250 students at the school would produce 64%.
The unsurveyed students must have the same opinions as the sample.
content.hint: Separate what was directly measured in the sample from what must be estimated about the population.
content.explanation: Right. The 64% is an exact description of the surveyed sample. It can estimate the population only with appropriate sampling and uncertainty.

blocks.html:
A good sample represents the target population

A sample is designed to be unbiased when its selection method does not systematically favor one kind of member over another.

On the SAT, the strongest design usually:

  • selects people randomly from the target population,
  • starts with a list or method that covers the whole target population, and
  • does not depend on people volunteering because they feel strongly.

A random sample does not have to look perfectly balanced by accident. Random selection makes the method fair; chance variation is handled with margin of error.

Recognize the common bias traps

  • Convenience sample: surveys whoever is easiest to reach, such as people at one location.
  • Voluntary-response sample: lets people choose themselves by clicking a poll or calling a number.
  • Undercoverage: leaves part of the target population out of the selection process.
  • Nonresponse bias: selected people who do not respond differ in a relevant way from those who do.

A large sample can still be biased. Ten thousand volunteers are not automatically more representative than a smaller random sample.

content.prompt: A city wants to estimate the opinions of all adult residents. Which method is most clearly biased?
choices: Randomly select adults from a complete city resident list.
Randomly select adults from each neighborhood in proportion to neighborhood size.
Randomly select addresses across the city and select one adult from each chosen household.
Invite visitors to the city website to choose whether to complete the survey.
content.hint: Which method allows people with strong opinions or frequent website use to select themselves?
content.explanation: Correct. Website visitors who volunteer may differ systematically from the full adult population, creating voluntary-response bias.

blocks.html:
Random selection is the start, not the whole survey

Some selected people may not respond. That does not automatically ruin a survey, but it can create bias if nonrespondents tend to answer differently from respondents. Follow-up attempts and multiple ways to respond can help.

The question itself should also be neutral. Compare:

  • Neutral: Do you support or oppose the proposed schedule?
  • Leading: Do you support the sensible proposed schedule?

Random selection cannot repair a question that pushes respondents toward an answer.

content.prompt: A company randomly selects customers for a satisfaction survey, but dissatisfied customers are much more likely to respond than satisfied customers. What is the main concern?
choices: The target population is too large to survey.
Nonresponse may bias the results because respondents differ from nonrespondents.
Random selection makes every response untrustworthy.
The company must survey every customer before making any estimate.
content.hint: The original selection was random, but compare the people who answered with those who did not.
content.explanation: Exactly. If response behavior is related to satisfaction, the respondents can overrepresent one opinion even though the initial sample was random.

blocks.html:
Find the largest population the results can describe

Some SAT questions ask: What is the largest population to which the survey results can be applied?

Look at the group from which participants were randomly selected. Keep every restriction in that description.

  • Randomly sampled from all eleventh-grade students in District K → all eleventh-grade students in District K
  • Randomly sampled from registered voters in County M → registered voters in County M
  • Randomly sampled from members of one gym → members of that gym

Decision rule: Generalize to the population represented by the random selection process—never to a broader group just because it seems similar.

content.prompt: A district randomly selects 300 students from a complete list of all eleventh-grade students in the district. What is the largest population to which the results can be generalized?
choices: All high school students in the state
All students in the district
All eleventh-grade students in the district
Only the 300 students who responded
content.hint: Preserve both restrictions in the selection group: grade level and district.
content.explanation: Correct. The random selection represents all eleventh-grade students in that district, but it does not represent other grades or other districts.

blocks.html:
Match the conclusion to the evidence

With an appropriately selected random sample, the sample statistic can estimate the corresponding value in the target population.

Good conclusions use language such as:

  • the data suggest that about this proportion of the population...
  • it is estimated that the population value is near...
  • it is plausible that the population value falls in a stated range...

The subject of the conclusion must match the target population, and the measured feature must match the survey question.

content.prompt: A random sample of registered voters in County M finds that 48% support a proposal. Which statement is best supported?
choices: The data suggest that about 48% of registered voters in County M support the proposal.
Exactly 48% of all County M residents support the proposal.
About 48% of registered voters throughout the country support the proposal.
Every future sample from County M will contain exactly 48% support.
content.hint: Keep the population as registered voters in County M and avoid claiming an exact population value.
content.explanation: Right. The conclusion keeps the correct target population and treats the sample result as an estimate rather than an exact fact.

blocks.html:
Know what the survey cannot prove

A survey result does not justify statements that:

  • claim the population percent is exactly the sample percent,
  • apply the result to a broader or different population,
  • claim every individual in the population has the majority opinion, or
  • claim that an observed opinion or behavior causes another outcome.

Sampling lets you estimate a population characteristic. It does not turn an estimate into certainty or a survey into a controlled experiment.

content.prompt: A well-designed random sample finds that 84% of sampled households use a recycling service. Which conclusion is not supported?
choices: The sample statistic is 84%.
The population proportion is likely near 84%.
The true population proportion may differ from 84%.
Exactly 84% of all households use the recycling service.
content.hint: Which choice incorrectly turns a sample estimate into an exact population fact?
content.explanation: Correct. The sample percentage is known, but the population percentage is estimated and may differ because of sampling variation.

blocks.html:
Margin of error describes sampling uncertainty

Even a fair random sample will not match the population perfectly every time. The margin of error describes a reasonable amount of sampling variation around the sample estimate.

If a survey reports 57% with a margin of error of 3 percentage points, use the sample percent as the center and move 3 points in both directions.

Plausible range: sample estimate − margin of error to sample estimate + margin of error

Use one subtraction and one addition

For 57% ± 3 percentage points:

  • lowest plausible value: 57% − 3 percentage points = 54%
  • highest plausible value: 57% + 3 percentage points = 60%

So the plausible range for the population proportion is 54% to 60%.

The SAT usually gives the margin of error. Your job is simply to create or interpret the interval, not to calculate the margin of error itself.

content.prompt: A random-sample survey reports 46% support with a margin of error of 5 percentage points. What is the plausible range for the population proportion?
content.hint: Subtract 5 points from 46 for the lower end, then add 5 points to 46 for the upper end.
content.explanation: Exactly. 46 − 5 = 41 and 46 + 5 = 51, so the plausible population range is 41% to 51%.

blocks.html:
The interval is plausible, not guaranteed

A margin-of-error interval gives a range of likely or plausible population values under the survey's statistical method. It does not prove that the true population value must fall inside that one interval.

The true population value can still be outside the reported range. That possibility is why careful answer choices say likely, plausible, or estimated instead of certain.

Watch out: Margin of error measures sampling uncertainty; it does not certify that the survey is unbiased or guarantee the population value.

content.prompt: A survey reports 62% with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which interpretation is most accurate?
choices: Exactly 62% of the population has the measured opinion.
The true population value must be between 58% and 66%.
Values from 58% to 66% are plausible, but the true population value could be outside that range.
Any value from 4% to 62% is equally likely.
content.hint: Build the interval, then choose wording that treats it as likely rather than guaranteed.
content.explanation: Correct. The margin of error creates a plausible interval of 58% to 66%, but a statistical interval is not an absolute guarantee.

blocks.html:
Increase the sample size to reduce margin of error

For the same survey design, the way to reduce the margin of error is to collect a larger random sample.

  • A larger sample gives a more precise estimate and a smaller margin of error.
  • A smaller sample gives a less precise estimate and a larger margin of error.

Changing the size of the population does not solve the problem. Changing from random selection to convenient selection does not help either.

Decision rule: If everything else stays the same, increase the sample size to reduce margin of error.

content.prompt: Researchers will repeat the same random-sample survey. Which change will reduce the margin of error?
choices: Increase the sample from 400 people to 1,600 people.
Survey the same 400 people with a more strongly worded question.
Replace the random sample with 400 volunteers.
Apply the results to a larger target population.
content.hint: Keep the survey design the same and change only how many randomly selected people are sampled.
content.explanation: Right. Increasing the random sample size reduces sampling variability and therefore reduces the margin of error.

blocks.html:
Do not confuse less uncertainty with less bias

Sample size and selection method solve different problems:

  • Random, representative selection protects against systematic bias.
  • Larger sample size reduces random sampling uncertainty and margin of error.

Increasing a biased sample can produce a more precise estimate of the wrong value. Margin of error also does not account for voluntary-response bias, undercoverage, leading wording, or serious nonresponse bias.

content.prompt: An online poll collects 10,000 voluntary responses. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The large sample guarantees that the poll represents the target population.
The poll has no uncertainty because more than 1,000 people responded.
A margin of error would automatically correct any voluntary-response bias.
The large sample does not remove bias caused by allowing respondents to select themselves.
content.hint: Ask whether adding more volunteers changes how those people entered the sample.
content.explanation: Correct. Sample size can improve precision, but it cannot fix a selection method that systematically overrepresents volunteers.

blocks.html:
Model the complete SAT process

A school district randomly selects 400 eleventh-grade students from its complete list of eleventh graders. Of the sampled students, 54% support a new tutoring period. The margin of error is 3 percentage points.

  1. Population: all eleventh-grade students in the district
  2. Sample quality: random selection from the complete target list
  3. Sample result: exactly 54% of the sample supports the plan
  4. Plausible population range: 51% to 57%
  5. Careful conclusion: support among all district eleventh graders is plausibly in that range, but it is not guaranteed

content.prompt: Which conclusion best matches the district survey?
choices: Exactly 54% of every student in the district supports the tutoring period.
It is plausible that 51% to 57% of the district's eleventh-grade students support the tutoring period.
At least 51% of all students in the state support the tutoring period.
The true support among district eleventh graders cannot be outside 51% to 57%.
content.hint: Keep the population as district eleventh graders, use the 51% to 57% range, and avoid a guarantee.
content.explanation: Exactly. This choice preserves the sampled population, uses the margin-of-error interval, and describes the range as plausible.

blocks.html:
Use the process without prompts

  1. Name: Identify the target population and sample.
  2. Audit: Check random selection, coverage, volunteering, nonresponse, and wording.
  3. Limit: Keep the conclusion inside the represented population and avoid exact certainty.
  4. Range: Subtract and add the margin of error, then call the interval plausible.

Use those four moves on the final questions.

content.prompt: A university randomly samples 250 students from a complete list of its first-year students. What is the largest population to which the results can be generalized?
choices: All university students in the country
All students at that university
All first-year students at that university
Only the 250 sampled first-year students
content.hint: Keep both restrictions from the selection list: first-year students and that university.
content.explanation: Correct. The random sample represents all first-year students at that university, not other class years or other universities.

content.prompt: A town randomly samples households from a complete address list, and 38% of the sampled households compost food waste. Which statement is best supported?
choices: The data suggest that about 38% of households in the town compost food waste.
Exactly 38% of households in the town compost food waste.
About 38% of households in the state compost food waste.
Composting food waste causes households to participate in surveys.
content.hint: Choose an estimate about the sampled target population, not an exact claim, broader population, or causal statement.
content.explanation: Right. The conclusion uses cautious language and stays within the town households represented by the random sample.

content.prompt: A valid random-sample survey reports 71% with a margin of error of 6 percentage points. Which population range is plausible?
content.hint: Subtract 6 from 71 for the lower end and add 6 to 71 for the upper end.
content.explanation: Correct. 71 − 6 = 65 and 71 + 6 = 77, so 65% to 77% is the plausible range.

content.prompt: Without looking back, which summary correctly describes the SAT survey process?
choices: Trust the largest sample, apply its exact result to similar groups, and treat the margin-of-error interval as guaranteed.
Identify the population, audit selection for bias, limit the claim to that population, and use plus/minus margin of error as a plausible—not guaranteed—range.
Ignore the selection method, calculate the population size, and subtract nonrespondents from the margin of error.
Apply every random sample to the whole country and reduce margin of error by rewriting the survey question.
content.hint: Retrieve the four moves: population, selection, claim, range.
content.explanation: You have it. A trustworthy inference begins with representative random selection, stays inside the represented population, and treats the margin-of-error interval as plausible rather than certain.

content.html:
You can reason through SAT surveys

You can identify biased sampling, find the largest population supported by a survey, choose appropriately cautious conclusions, build a margin-of-error range, and explain why larger samples improve precision without repairing bias.
